title: AI advocacy: Assistance claims exceed victory evidence
desc: Distinguishes digital moot support from decisive Supreme Court impact, raising separate attribution, disclosure and reputational questions.

kps.k: The dispute turns on the gap between AI-assisted preparation and claims that AI helped determine a Supreme Court victory.
kps.d: Katyal says a bespoke Harvey system used 25 years of judicial questions and writings to anticipate questions, suggest responses and identify reasoning that could attract Chief Justice Roberts’s support in the tariffs case. His evidence includes retrospective comparisons of predicted questions with the argument transcript and a claimed near-verbatim prediction of Gorsuch’s separate opinion. These accounts illustrate a proposed use of AI, but neither the reported 6–3 victory nor the comparisons independently establish predictive accuracy or causal influence. The ABA Journal account draws on Bloomberg Law rather than supplying independent confirmation.

qs.q: And I trained it on every question asked by a Supreme Court justice in the last 25 years  and everything they've written, every opinion, every concurrence, every dissent, every separate opinion.
qs.a: What really won the trillion-dollar Supreme Court case (TED Talk transcript) · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: In the TED Talk, Katyal displayed Harvey’s predicted questions alongside excerpts from the actual oral argument transcript, saying some were “almost verbatim.” He also credited the tool with identifying an “escape route” to bring Chief Justice John Roberts to his side in the case.
qs.a: Katyal's Boast of AI Role in Tariff Win Draws Swift Blowback · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Supporters frame judicial prediction as augmentation, not a substitute for an advocate’s judgment.
kps.d: Harvey’s company blog presents Harvey Moot as a preparation partner developed with Katyal’s team and describes its contribution as a small part of intensive preparation. Katyal argues that courtroom advocacy still requires composure, connection and independent real-time decisions; he warns against simply repeating AI output. He and Mitu Gulati interpret predictable judicial reasoning as evidence of principled consistency, while Daniel Epps worries that the presentation implied an ability to manipulate judicial votes. Lat’s anecdote about a human-reviewed ChatGPT message offers a limited counterpoint to categorical claims that interpersonal assistance lies beyond AI, not evidence of courtroom substitution.

qs.q: But what he and his team saw was notable: the opportunity for Harvey to be a sparring partner, anticipating not just the likely questions and responses from the Justices, but also how he might consider responding in a manner that resonates.
qs.a: The Supreme Case for Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But if I had just parroted Harvey's output,  I would have lost the case 10-0,  and there aren't even 10 justices.
qs.a: What really won the trillion-dollar Supreme Court case (TED Talk transcript) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Critics challenge decisive-impact claims and individual credit without necessarily rejecting digital moot courts.
kps.d: Epps disputes that AI and coaching supplied the decisive difference; Gulati doubts oral argument changed votes despite recognising potential value in prediction tools. Wang stresses the collective work behind Supreme Court litigation while predicting wider use of digital moot courts and reporting his own use. Lat says many commentators expected the administration to lose before argument and reports Sarah Isgur’s concerns about apparent transcript discrepancies. These objections do not establish a measured failure rate. Criticism of omitted credit also requires qualification: Katyal’s promotional post thanked his legal team and the Liberty Justice Center, and he told Lat that teamwork and vulnerability were central to his intended message.

qs.q: “The notion that it’s Katyal’s preparation with his mindfulness coach and AI that was the key difference maker, I just think people think that was a little preposterous,” said Daniel Epps, a professor at the Washington University School of Law in St.
qs.a: Katyal's Boast of AI Role in Tariff Win Draws Swift Blowback · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: “Everybody reads everything and it’s hard to imagine oral argument changed anybody’s vote,” Gulati said.
qs.a: Katyal's Boast of AI Role in Tariff Win Draws Swift Blowback · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: AI victory narratives raise disclosure and reputational questions distinct from technical effectiveness.
kps.d: Lat asked whether Katyal had a material connection to Harvey requiring disclosure. Katyal denied compensation, discounts or incentives and said he was a paying customer; Harvey denied a promotional arrangement or equity holding. These attributed statements do not establish a disclosure violation or constitute an independent financial audit. Williams draws a communications lesson: law firms should temper technology claims, disclose relevant relationships and credit clients and collaborators. Negative online reactions and Lat’s reader poll describe reception, not AI effectiveness or representative professional opinion; Lat also rejects predictions that the episode would end Katyal’s Supreme Court career.

qs.q: A spokeswoman for Harvey said in an email it has no arrangement with Katyal to promote its services and he doesn’t hold any investment or equity stake in the company.
qs.a: Katyal's Boast of AI Role in Tariff Win Draws Swift Blowback · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: For law‑firm marketers, the lesson is clear – AI war stories are powerful content, but the tone, disclosures and allocation of credit; ber they to clients, co‑counsel, funders and yes, the humans on the team matter just as much as the technology itself.
qs.a: Neal Katyal, Harvey AI and the Supreme Court TED-Gate · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Broader educational and access-to-justice benefits remain prospective.
kps.d: Harvey uses its Supreme Court preparation experiences to advocate wider appellate and classroom adoption, including partnerships with law school faculty and students. It links those ambitions to a stated access-to-justice goal. The material supplies practitioner experiences and vendor aspirations, not measured improvements in student learning, advocacy outcomes or unmet civil legal need. The practical proposition is to explore AI-supported rehearsal while keeping claims about adoption, performance and social benefit separate.

qs.q: That includes working with the industry to power how AI changes the landscape, but also more broadly building partnerships with law school faculty and students to help empower the next generation of lawyers for a meaningfully different way of thinking and working.
qs.a: The Supreme Case for Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: We hope they are the first of many teams to use Harvey to strengthen case preparation, whether at the highest levels of appellate advocacy or in the classroom.
qs.a: The Supreme Case for Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the proposition that AI-assisted advocacy preparation should be distinguished from evidence that AI determined a Supreme Court victory. Harvey presents Harvey Moot as an augmentative “sparring partner” for anticipating questions and refining responses, while expressly characterising its role in the tariffs case as small rather than decisive. The source also separates demonstrated use from prospective benefit: its claims about wider appellate adoption, legal education and access to justice are framed as ambitions or potential, not measured outcomes. Internal variation lies mainly in emphasis: the account is cautious about causal attribution in the specific case but more promotional when generalising from that experience to future case preparation, classrooms and social benefit. Because this facet contains one curated vendor source, it supports a source-specific conclusion rather than a claim about legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: But what he and his team saw was notable: the opportunity for Harvey to be a sparring partner, anticipating not just the likely questions and responses from the Justices, but also how he might consider responding in a manner that resonates.
qs.a: The Supreme Case for Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: We were honored to be a small part of their intense preparation, but what we are most proud of is the potential this work creates for our academic partnerships and for future case preparation.
qs.a: The Supreme Case for Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated sources in this professional-voice grouping support the proposition that Harvey may have assisted Supreme Court preparation, but that the available material does not establish independently measured predictive accuracy or a decisive effect on the outcome. Their common reasons are that the performance claims are retrospective and largely Katyal’s own; the Justices may already have been inclined toward the result; oral argument is only one part of collective litigation; and predicted-question comparisons do not demonstrate causation. They also consistently separate technical usefulness from attribution, disclosure and reputational concerns. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis: Williams foregrounds communications, shared credit and hype; Fischer balances skepticism about decisive impact with expectations that digital moot courts will spread; Lat probes transcript discrepancies, prior expectations and possible material connections while accepting carefully reviewed AI assistance; Katyal advances the strongest victory-linked predictive claims, but still frames Harvey as augmentation requiring independent human judgment. Thus, the overall position is supportive rather than mixed, while Katyal’s account remains a significant internal qualification and the selected sources should not be treated as representative of all press or market commentary.

vlens.an: Within this curated professional-body voice, the ABA Journal report supports the proposition that evidence of AI-assisted preparation does not establish that AI determined the Supreme Court victory. It reports Katyal’s prediction claims as attributed assertions rather than independently validated findings and contrasts them with objections that the outcome also reflected extensive collective legal work and may not have been affected by oral argument. The principal internal variation concerns utility rather than causation: Gulati recognises potential value in AI prediction tools while doubting that the argument changed any justice’s vote, whereas Epps more sharply rejects the portrayal of AI and coaching as the decisive difference. Thus, the source leaves room for Harvey as an augmentation tool but does not substantiate predictive accuracy or causal impact on the judgment. This assessment applies to the supplied source and should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: The system was built by Harvey AI, which “predicted many of the questions the justices asked—sometimes almost word for word,” Katyal said in an X post promoting the TED Talk.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources overall support the proposition that evidence for AI-assisted advocacy preparation is stronger than evidence that Harvey decisively affected the Supreme Court victory. The common basis is evidentiary: the materials document use of a bespoke digital moot tool and Katyal’s retrospective claims that it anticipated questions and reasoning, but provide neither a systematic accuracy evaluation nor an independent causal analysis separating Harvey’s contribution from the justices’ prior views, oral advocacy, co-counsel, briefs and other preparation. Several sources also accept the narrower augmentation case: AI may serve as a sparring partner or peripheral vision while human judgment remains in the loop. Material variation concerns how strongly the victory narrative is advanced. Harvey’s company account describes its role as small and treats educational and access-to-justice benefits as prospective; journalistic and commentary sources more directly question decisive impact, individual credit and promotional framing while allowing that digital moot courts may be useful. Katyal’s own account is the principal mixed element: he makes strong retrospective prediction claims linked to the result, yet expressly rejects uncritical reliance on Harvey’s output. Disclosure, shared-credit and reputational concerns reinforce the proposition’s distinction between technical effectiveness and communications issues. Because these are selected sources, this alignment should not be read as representative of all advocates, commentators or legal-AI providers in 2026.
